reviews.author: jang ramul
reviews.text:
A fusion Japanese wine bar that recently reopened in Insa-dong. I went there when I was in Hannam-dong and I remember enjoying the food, so I was glad to hear that it had reopened.

The menu features many dishes based on raw seafood, and the wine lineup reflects the owner's tastes and has a solid natural wine lineup. Although alcoholic beverages are required to be ordered, glass and non-alcoholic drinks are also available, and corkage is available for 30,000 won.
--------
♤ Sashimi Noodle (23,000₩)
It's buckwheat soba with truffle and sashimi added. At first, the truffle scent is attractive, then moves on to the taste of tsuyu, and ends with the salmon and flying fish roe popping. A unique and delicious menu that will captivate your eyes, nose, and mouth.

♤ Samran Pasta (21,000₩)
This is a menu that everyone will like, regardless of likes or dislikes. It is a perilla oil pasta made with three types of eggs: poached eggs, cod roe, and fish roe. In addition to the eggs, seaweed and green onions add flavor. It was the same as before when I visited, and it was the most delicious menu I had.

♤ Sashimi Konowada (23,000₩)
A menu where you dip sashimi in konowada (salted fish with sea cucumber intestines). Although Konowada smells like the sea, it doesn't have a fishy smell and it's savory and delicious. However, due to the nature of the ingredients, there seems to be quite a bit of likes and dislikes, so I recommend this only to those who enjoy sea cucumber.
--------
The owner was good at recommending and explaining wine, and although the interior was small, it wasn't crowded or noisy, which was nice. Instead, it is recommended to make a reservation and visit as there are limited seats.

It is located on the second floor of the building, so you can enjoy the view down the Insa-dong street below from the window seat where the full-length windows are open. The interior is decorated with a variety of traditional items that give off an old-fashioned feel, creating a comfortable atmosphere that matches well with modern lighting. I like that the individual and group seats are appropriately prepared and cleanly maintained. We sell craft beer from Ganadara Brewery, a local brewery in Mungyeong, Gyeongsangbuk-do. It's fun because they provide mini yakgwa as a basic snack. They sell a wide variety of traditional teas, sweet red bean porridge, and various types of shaved ice, as well as a variety of beer snacks such as chicken, pizza, and french fries. You can also order premium shochu, sake, and highball. I like the staff's good sense and friendly response. It's a store with a unique concept, but I'm satisfied.

Bona Jewelry Museum is the largest specialized jewelry museum in Korea, established to preserve and publicize the jewelry of our ancient women.
The Bona Jewelry Museum, established based on over 10,000 artifacts that Director Kim Myung-hee has carefully collected over the past 40 years, is operated in Gwanhun-dong, Jongno-gu, Seoul. Recognized as the 35th private museum registered by the Seoul Metropolitan Government in 2006, Bona is receiving a lot of media attention as a museum symbolizing our unique beauty that shines like a jewel.
Not only does it display about 200 pieces of jewelry and lifestyle-related artifacts from each era, including men's and women's accessories and Goryeo Dynasty dress styles and buttons to early modern playthings, allowing visitors to appreciate the history and culture of Korean jewelry in one place, but it also holds a special exhibition of the collection once or twice a year to allow visitors to appreciate new cultural assets, and is carrying out various exhibitions and research activities to provide a broad understanding of women's jewelry culture.
This is to feel and share the beauty and taste of ancient women with more people, and to help young people who will protect and lead our culture in the future discover the value of our beauty by inheriting our unique beauty and spirit, preserve it as a foundation, and create new beauty in a more advanced way.
In addition, we will do our best to establish ourselves as a cultural space where people can experience and share our cultural assets that have been preserved by our ancestors.

reviews.text: The General Bureau of Posts is located right next to Jogyesa Temple, a famous temple in Korea, near Jonggak Station. The General Bureau of Posts was founded in 1884 by Hong Yeong-sik, a civil servant of the Enlightenment faction in the late Joseon Dynasty. It is the first modern post office in Korea, established to introduce postal services. It is said that part of the current General Bureau of Posts building was built on the site of the former General Bureau of Posts. The Post Office Museum explains how Korea's first modern post office was established and developed in the late Joseon Dynasty, and displays information about Hong Yeong-sik, an enlightenment school official, and various stamps. There are two types of stamps: commemorative stamps and regular stamps. It is said that commemorative stamps are issued when commemorating national events such as the 1988 Olympics. It is said that a stamp is attached to a piece of mail in the form of a small piece of paper indicating that the mailing fee has been paid in advance and is used to signify that the mailing fee has been paid in advance. Nowadays, the sender pays the postage fee, but due to various unreasonable postage rates, the method has changed to the method where the sender pays the postage fee in advance. It would be nice to visit Jogyesa Temple, a famous Korean temple, and Insa-dong, where you can feel Korean tradition, while looking at the old Post Office.

reviews.text:
A government office in charge of postal services during the late Joseon Dynasty.

content
It was established on March 27, 1884 (the 21st year of King Gojong's reign), and Hong Yeong-sik (洪英植) was appointed as the person in charge on March 28, and prepared for the opening of the country by preparing laws. Postal services began for the first time on October 1 of that year. The position consisted of one person each, Chief Judge and Bangpan, and 3 divisions and 15 departments under them. The three departments were planning department, arrival and departure department, and calculation department.

In May 1884, two Japanese practitioners were hired. It was planned to have the General Bureau of Posts at the center, and to establish post offices in each region (in fact, the Incheon branch was established in Incheon), post office, and post office. The Post Office headquarters was located in Jeondong. It was established as an independent organization, and its relationship with other government offices is unknown.

It was abolished on December 8, 1884 (October 21 in the lunar calendar), because the Gapsin Coup took place on December 4 (October 17 in the lunar calendar) using the celebration of the opening of the Post Office, but failed. However, even after the abolition, the postal service continued, and the postal service actually closed on November 20th of the lunar calendar, and the Incheon branch office was closed only on December 1st of the lunar calendar.

Significance and Evaluation
After its abolition, there was discussion of its revival, but it was not until 1893 that it was renamed the Comrade General Bureau, followed by the Gongmu-Amun Post Office in 1894, the Agriculture, Commerce and Education Bureau in 1895, and the Correspondent Bureau in 1900. It is easy to emphasize that the Post Office was the first modern postal institution and its connection with the Gapsin Coup, but it also had many limitations.

In other words, the General Post seems to have focused on international postal services rather than domestic postal services. Before starting domestic postal services, it had already promoted the conclusion of postal exchange treaties with foreign countries, signed agreements with Japan and Hong Kong in April, and was also pursuing membership in the Universal Postal Union (UPU). It is acknowledged that since the establishment of the postal office in Busan in November 1876, attempts have been made to eliminate the Japanese postal organization that had its own postal route in Joseon.
[Encyclopedia of Korean National Culture]

Heidi Buher: Space is a membrane, a skin.
2023. 03. 28 ~ 2023. 06. 25

Art Sonje Center is hosting Asia's first retrospective exhibition of Swiss female avant-garde artist Heidi Bucher from March 28 to June 25. Heidi Bucher caused a stir in the international art world through a large-scale retrospective exhibition held at the Haus der Kunst in Munich, Germany, held in 2021. Haus de Kunst director Andrea Lissoni described Heidi Buchher as a “game changer” in the history of modernist sculpture. This exhibition was later toured at the Bern Museum and the Susch Museum in Switzerland, and the British Frieze magazine selected the Susch Museum's Heidi Bucher exhibition as one of the top 10 exhibitions in Europe in 2022.

Booher’s art world explores the human body and its mode of existence located in a specific space through sculptural and performative work methods under a clear theme of ‘liberation’. Booher explored spaces with inherent patriarchal hierarchy, such as his father's study, the floorboards of the house where his ancestors lived for generations, and the treatment room of Dr Binswanger, a psychiatrist who, along with Freud, was the leading expert of his time on the disease called hysteria, which was based on misogyny. Her work intervened in these spaces through skinning, a technique of applying latex, covering it with cloth, and then peeling it off. Buher explained the installation work using this skinning technique as ‘the act of creating skin,’ where the skin was presented as an interface with the world and a sensory storehouse of memories containing joy and pain, happiness and discomfort. This exhibition presents four major skinning installation works, including (1988), (1980), and (1976), created by Buheo using the skinning technique.

《Heidi Bucher: Space is a Film, Skin》 is a large-scale retrospective exhibition that includes approximately 130 drawings, sculptures, installations, and video records, including drawings and archives showing Bucher's early work world, up to her later skinning installation works. Major works include four major skinning installation works, including (1988), (1980), and (1976), created by Buheo using the skinning technique. Booher's work, which sought to reveal the hierarchy inherent in social and personal space and create a space for change, is a long journey toward liberation that reveals, as she puts it, a “process of metamorphosis.” Through this exhibition, we hope to confirm that the challenges and adventures of a female artist who has been forgotten in neo-avant-garde art history since the 1960s have not ended even now in the 21st century, and to create a space for new transformation.

- Excerpt from the exhibition introduction on the website

Gwanmulcheo is a place with a particularly quiet and calm atmosphere among Changdeokgung Palace. The wooden building and the open garden were in harmony, and I was struck by the sense that time was passing slowly. The view from the large window was particularly elegant, even among palaces, and it was impressive to be able to enjoy the beauty of the four seasons.
When I visited, the colorful leaves scattered in the wind in the garden, and I was able to truly relax while looking at the beautiful scenery from the window. The Gwanmulcheo not only allows you to feel the traditional Korean architectural beauty, but also has a deep sense of tranquility that allows you to imagine how the kings of the time lived, allowing you to feel the weight of history.
In addition, there are many valuable cultural assets on display in the museum, so I knew very well that it was not just a tourist attraction, but a place where you could actually come into contact with the history. reviews.text:
Buddhist Institute Foundation (Seonhakwon)
After the opening of ports in 1876, Japanese Buddhism took advantage of imperialism's policy of aggression.
He promoted the subordination of Korean national Buddhism.
In October 1910, Lee Hoi-gwang, the Korean representative of the Wonjong Order, signed an agreement with the Japanese Soto Sect in Tokyo, the imperialist metropolis of Japan.
Accordingly, Jin Eung and Han Yeong, Korean ethnic Buddhists, established the Imje Order (任制宗) at Jeungsimsa Temple in Gwangju.
On February 3, 1911, a temporary founding office of the Joseon Imjejong Order was established at Songgwangsa Temple and Gyeongwoongi (景雲元基) was appointed as the general director.
Moreover, in order to control and reduce Korean national Buddhism to Japanese style, Japan enacted a control system for Korean or Joseon Buddhism called the Buddhist Temple Management Ordinance on June 3, 1911.
In response to this, on May 2, 1912, the Joseon Imjejong changed its administrative system from the existing temporary founding temple to the Central Missionary Office and moved to Insa-dong, Seoul.
However, Japanese imperialism hindered the establishment of the Central Missionary Center and the activities of the Joseon Imjejong Order.
Prominent national Buddhists such as Han Yong-un and Baek Yong-seong participated as national Buddhist leaders in the March 1st Movement in 1919.
Many other Buddhist believers and students also actively participated in this movement.
In particular, Han Yong-un wrote three articles of pledge regarding the March 1st Movement and included it in the Declaration of Independence.
Additionally, in Shanghai in November, the Korean Buddhist Confirmation of Ascension, written in Korean, Chinese, and English, was distributed around the world.
Such passionate participation and action revealed the strong will of Korean Buddhism.
On November 30, 1921, Namjun, Dobong, and Seokdu joined the independence movement with Han Yongun, not only preventing the country from falling into Japanese-style Buddhism, but also resisting the secularization of national Buddhism. It also invalidated the so-called Japanese-style temple crackdown order. Lastly, the National Reformed Buddhist Academy Foundation was established to protect and maintain Korean Buddhism.
In March 1922, Han Yong-un and Oh Seong-wol established the Zen Buddhist Cooperative to protect national Buddhism against Japan's colonial Buddhism policy.
With the First Je sitz Congress in 1931, Seonhakwon Buddhists did their best to protect national Buddhism and spread Buddhist faith. Also, through this struggle, Seonhakwon was able to establish the Joseon Seon Buddhist Research and Action Center on December 5, 1934.
In 1935, at the Third Jeondae Congress, Seonhakwon and Buddhists founded the Joseon Seon Buddhism, which later became a symbol of Korean national Buddhism against Japanese colonial rule. And in 1941, a Buddhist protection ceremony was held.
After liberation, Seonhakwon cleared away the remnants of the Japanese colonial period.
We tried to preserve Korean Buddhist traditions. On June 24, 1954, Seonhakwon first held a conference to promote the Korean Reformed Buddhist Movement, and the next day formed a Preparatory Committee for the Reformed Buddhist Movement.
On August 24-25, Seonhakwon first held a national Buddhist representative conference and elected monks such as Geumo, Jeokeum, Dongsan, Cheongdam, and Hyobong as members of the Buddhist executive committee.
In August 1955, following the holding of the then-National Buddhist Representative Conference, Seonhakwon's administrative control and operational authority over temples across the country were transferred to the monks.
Ultimately, Seonhakwon continued its efforts to protect national Buddhism.
